deep.reconstruction:
There is no mathematics on this page. It is a page of German-language notes on ancient history: the period of the Diadochi (Alexander's successors). It may be lecture notes or excerpts. Neither the hand nor the layout looks like Gauss's mathematical working papers, so these could be copied lecture notes bound into the Nachlass.

Content of the page:
- Heading: 'Zweiter Zeitabschnitt. Vom Tode des Perdiccas bis zum Tode des Eumenes. 321 – 315.' (Second period: from the death of Perdiccas to the death of Eumenes, 321–315.)
- Once Antipater became regent, a new division of the provinces was made by him at Triparadisus in Syria.
- Ptolemy kept Egypt, Antipater took Macedonia and Seleucus took Babylonia.
- Antigonus received Phrygia, Lycia and Pamphylia, together with Cappadocia, the land of Eumenes, who was declared an outlaw ('in die Acht erklärt').
- Antigonus, a native Macedonian, now became supreme commander. He was already 60 years old. He had outstanding talents as a general, but his pride would bow to no one.
- The page ends 'Er verstand sich', which continues on folio 144 ('wohl die Kunst zu regieren…').

This continues folio 142 (death of Perdiccas in 321, Antipater elected regent) and leads into folio 144 (Antigonus's character, his son Demetrius Poliorcetes).

No derivation exists to reconstruct.
errors: No mathematical errors, since there is no mathematics.
Historical content: the settlement of Triparadisus (321/320 BC) did assign Babylonia to Seleucus and confirm Ptolemy in Egypt.

Antigonus did retain Greater Phrygia, Lycia and Pamphylia and was given the royal army to fight Eumenes, who was outlawed; Cappadocia was Eumenes' satrapy. The notes' wording 'nebst Cappadocien' is loose but compatible with this.
Antigonus (born c. 382 BC) being about 60 in 321 is roughly correct.
Eumenes' death date 315 follows the older chronology; modern dating is usually 316 BC.

results.what: Narrative notes on the partition of Triparadisus and the character of Antigonus Monophthalmus
results.usually_credited_to: Standard historical material from ancient sources (Diodorus, Arrian's Events after Alexander) as conveyed in early-19th-century lectures

deep.surprise_reason: The page is purely historical narrative with no mathematical content. It is routine lecture or excerpt material on Hellenistic history, and possibly not even in Gauss's hand.

checkable.asserts: The heading's period 321–315 spans six years (trivial; there is no mathematical content to verify).
If Antigonus was born c. 381/382 BC, he was about 60 at Triparadisus in 321, consistent with the text.

transcription_corrections: 'Trisparadisus' is as written in the manuscript, but the correct place name is Triparadisus (Triparadeisos).
The line 'Antigonus. Phrygien, Lycien, Pamphylien' carries 'nebst' as a superscript insertion before 'u Cappadocien', so it reads 'Antigonus: Phrygien, Lycien, Pamphylien nebst Cappadocien'.
'wurde jetzt Oberfeldherr' — the final word is written in a cramped form above the line; 'Oberfeldherr' is plausible but uncertain.
'Er besass ausgezeichnete Feldherrn Talente' — the word before 'Feldherrn' may be 'ausgezeichnete' (it looks like 'ein[e] ausgezeichnete'); 'Feldherrn Talente' itself is fairly secure.
'aber sein Stolz ließ sich vor Niemand beugen' — reading 'Stolz', 'ließ', 'beugen' appears correct from the image.
